samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both are dark, self-contained viewers in a monospace face at about 13px. Both use aligned timestamp, level and component columns and mark WARN/ERROR rows with a tinted band and a left edge bar. In both, the long WARN/ERROR lines wrap onto a second line with a hanging indent instead of scrolling horizontally, so neither fully meets item 2. A adds line numbers and B adds a 'Problems only' filter, which roughly cancel out. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers show the log in a dark monospace layout at about 13px. Both use fixed columns for time, level and job, and mark WARN/ERROR lines with a colored background band and a left border, so they rely on more than color alone. In both, the longer WARN/ERROR lines wrap onto a second line with a hanging indent instead of scrolling sideways. B adds line numbers and A highlights unusual values; otherwise they are nearly the same in quality. The screenshots can't confirm item 5, so both are scored on the assumption that each is a self-contained file.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers wrap the long ERROR entry onto a second line, which breaks the one-line-per-entry requirement. A is worse on that row: its timestamp column is too narrow, so '02:00:12' splits into '02:00:1 / 2', and the longer ERROR word pushes the component and message columns out of line. B keeps the timestamp, level and component columns aligned on every row, and marks WARN and ERROR rows with a left bar, a background band and bold text, so it is the better answer. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both use a dark monospace layout with background bands, edge markers and bold level words for WARN and ERROR. Both wrap the long ERROR line. In B the wrap is worse: the timestamp breaks into '02:00:1' / '2', and the ERROR level, component and field columns shift out of line with the other rows. A keeps every column aligned and only the trailing field wraps, so it reads more cleanly overall.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): A keeps every entry on one line and scrolls horizontally. Its WARN/ERROR rows get a background band, a left-edge marker and bold text, and the level words line up in a column. B looks similar but wraps the long WARN/ERROR lines into ragged continuation lines, which breaks the one-entry-per-line scanning the request needs. B is still easy to read because it uses slightly looser spacing and shows the full timestamps. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B keeps each entry on a single line and scrolls horizontally, so the columns stay intact. A wraps the long WARN and ERROR entries onto ragged continuation lines, which is the exact failure rubric item 2 describes. Both use a comfortable monospace face, aligned level columns, background bands with a left marker for problems, and appear self-contained; B's lines are slightly tighter and it drops the date from the timestamp, but neither hurts scanning.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover every rubric problem and give full corrected CSS. B wins on two points. It says what matters most first (line length), and it correctly notes that Georgia has no lining or tabular figures, so A's `font-variant-numeric` fix on Georgia would do nothing. B's one weak spot is the shaky claim that the browser fakes Georgia's bold italic, since Georgia does ship a bold italic face. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers catch nearly every real problem and give full corrected CSS. A ranks its fixes from biggest win to smallest and starts with line length. It also correctly says Georgia cannot supply lining or tabular figures, while B's `font-variant-numeric` fix on Georgia will do nothing. A's one weak point is a dubious claim that Georgia lacks a usable bold italic, and B's link between justified text and narrow columns doesn't match this layout's very wide column.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers catch every real problem in the CSS: line length, leading, tracking, justification, the backwards h1, the unspaced uppercase tag, and the invisible links. B ranks its fixes from most to least damaging and names the two that matter most, so it scores better on prioritization. A wrongly claims Georgia has no true bold italic, which counts as an invented problem; B's suggestion of tabular-nums is probably ineffective on Georgia, but that is a smaller slip. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers find all the main problems and give good corrected CSS. A explicitly ranks the fixes from most to least damaging and names the two that matter most. B says Georgia has no true bold italic, which is false because Georgia ships a Bold Italic face. B also replaces the font for prices, which goes beyond what the CSS actually shows is wrong. A's tabular-nums suggestion may have no effect in Georgia, but that is a minor slip, not a made-up problem.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers find every real problem in the CSS and give a full corrected snippet with sensible values. A edges ahead on accuracy: it warns that Georgia may have no lining figures, so `lining-nums` may do nothing. B uses `lining-nums` with Georgia without that warning, and adds extras the CSS didn't call for (`font-synthesis`, right-aligned prices, a complaint about heading margins that aren't in the CSS). A's contrast note is a hedge rather than a claim that the color fails, but it is still slightly off-topic. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers find every real problem and give full replacement CSS. B edges ahead with a clear 'if you change only three things' list and an accurate caveat that Georgia may not support lining-nums, while A applies lining-nums without that caveat. B's hedged contrast remark adds nothing, but it does not claim the contrast fails.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers use different figures for the table and the sentences, and both give correct font-variant-numeric CSS with right alignment for the table. B allows old-style figures in the prose, which gives the designer a sensible place for them. It also covers font support more thoroughly, including the risk that subsetting strips the OpenType features. A rules out old-style figures entirely, which is defensible but less balanced, and its font-support note is thinner. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers split the table from the dashboard sentences and give working font-variant-numeric CSS with tabular lining figures for the right-aligned table. A sets old-style figures for sentences where the reader compares $4,820.50 with $3,990.00, and it probably wrongly says Inter has old-style figures. B uses proportional lining figures there, explains why, and adds useful notes on fixed decimals and overriding fonts that default to old-style figures.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers separate the table from the dashboard sentences and recommend right-aligned tabular lining figures for the table. B's CSS is more careful: it right-aligns only the numeric columns, while A also right-aligns the description column and makes old-style figures the global default on body. B also explains what happens when a font lacks the figure styles (the setting is silently ignored) and gives a concrete test, while A covers font support well but gives no way to check it. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers use tabular lining figures for the table and proportional figures for the dashboard sentences. Answer A has cleaner CSS because it right-aligns only the numeric columns, while Answer B right-aligns every table cell, including descriptions. Answer B is more candid about font support: it notes Inter's limited old-style figures and the risk that font subsetting drops these features, and it offers a font-feature-settings fallback. That roughly balances A's tidier code.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers treat the table and the sentences separately and give sound CSS. B describes the old-style digit shapes correctly, fairly gives the designer the prose case, and explains font support most concretely, including Wakamai Fondue, silent fallback to lining figures, and fonts that default to old-style. A wrongly says 6 drops below the baseline and 3 and 5 rise, and its font check is thinner. B's closing advice to default to tabular contradicts its own body-level old-style CSS, but that is a smaller flaw. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers handle the split correctly: tabular lining figures for the table and proportional figures in the sentences. A also correctly says which old-style digits drop below the baseline and which rise, and gives a concrete way to check the font for missing features. B wrongly describes the old-style digits (it says 4 and 6 drop, and 3 and 5 rise). A's body-level CSS also contradicts its own advice to make tabular lining the default, but B's factual mistake weighs more.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers are three plain-language sentences that correctly explain that large type gets tightened because the gaps look loose, while text-size type is already spaced for reading. B edges ahead on the concrete-touchpoint item because it says what happens if you tighten paragraph text (long text gets harder to read), whereas A only says designers leave it alone. B's phrase 'look wider than they really are' is slightly imprecise, but neither answer gives wrong guidance. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers are three plain-language sentences, and neither gives wrong guidance. B explains the cause more clearly: default letter spacing is designed for small text, so the gaps look loose at headline size. A only says the gaps 'look wider than they really are', which describes the effect without explaining why it happens.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B gives the actual reason in plain words: gaps between letters grow with the letters, so big headlines look loose and gappy. It also shows the reader what goes wrong if you tighten paragraph text, since the letters 'run together'. A is accurate and shorter, but its 'viewed from a distance' explanation is less direct about why size matters, and 'harder to read' is vaguer; B loses only a little for its 'Here's a draft' lead-in line. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A gives the real reason in plain words: gaps grow along with the letters, so big headlines look loose and gappy, while paragraph text is already spaced to read well and tightening it would make the letters run together. B is shorter, but it puts the problem down to uneven gaps seen from a distance rather than gaps that grow with size, and its picture of what goes wrong is less concrete. A's one-line 'Here's a draft you can paste' lead-in costs it a little on length, but the pasteable message itself is three sentences.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers are three plain sentences with no wrong guidance. B explains the actual cause more clearly: spacing is tuned for reading sizes, so the gaps grow when the type is enlarged, and its 'loose and gappy' image is easy to picture. A gives a slightly more concrete picture of what tightening paragraph text does (letters crowd together), but it only says the gaps 'look too loose' at large sizes without saying why. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers are three plain sentences with no wrong guidance. A gives a clearer reason: spacing is tuned for reading sizes, so the gaps scale up and look loose when the type is blown up. B only says the default gaps look too loose at a huge size, but it does give a concrete picture of tightened paragraph text crowding together, which A leaves vaguer.

Answer B marks its assumptions more consistently with [confirm], but it gives no guidance on how type behaves across screen widths. Neither answer explains what the dev should expect if Inter fails to load. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers are well structured and cover every style. B is better on scalable units, with unitless line heights next to the px source values. It also does more on screen width, using a 65ch measure, text-wrap and a 320px test, and covers more link states and gives a concrete check with Inter blocked. A flags its assumptions more consistently, while B leaves the label tracking and a few rules, such as prices at body size, unflagged.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers cover every style in a scannable table with rem sizes and unitless line heights, and both flag the title tightening, label tracking and tabular figures as values to confirm. A is stronger on link states, with hover, visited and focus written out in CSS, and on narrow and wide screens, with balanced wrapping, a 65ch line-length cap and tests at 320px and 200% zoom. A also leaves the colors as placeholders. B invents hex values (marked to confirm) and says only that one set of sizes applies at all breakpoints. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover every style in clear tables, with rem sizes and unitless line heights. B goes further on behaviour across screen sizes: text-wrap, a 65ch measure, a 320px test and zoom checks. It also gives full CSS for all link states and uses placeholders for colors instead of inventing hex values. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B clearly flags every assumption, including title tracking, label values, placeholder colors, button line-height, hover style and breakpoints, and gathers them into a confirm list for the designer. Its line-height ratios are precise, and it mentions font-display: swap and checking the fallback font. A is richer on responsive behavior (no fluid scaling, 65ch measure, text-wrap, a 320px test) and on link states, but it doesn't mark the title tracking as proposed and rounds 28/22 to 1.275. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover every style in a clear table with rem values and unitless line heights. A marks every value it had to fill in (title tracking, label specs, colours, breakpoints) as [CONFIRM] and lists them at the end, and its checklist tells the dev to check the fallback fonts. B adds more on spacing, wide-screen behaviour and link states, but it presents the title tracking and the 'no fluid scaling' choice as decided rather than proposed, and it never says what to check if Inter fails to load.
